clue.text: This woman, they say, needs my body

definitions.text: This woman, they say, needs my body

blocks.clueFragment: This woman, they say, needs my body
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who is said to want the speaker, a love-sick line
setter's reading: heard aloud, needs is kneads, so this is a woman who works the muscles of the body

explanation.surface: Someone boasts that a certain woman is reported to be desperate for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They say' tells you to hear 'needs' as 'kneads': a MASSEUSE kneads your body for a living.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman whose profession is massage works the client's muscles with her hands.

clue.text: "Maverick", valedictory Western role for Monroe or Gable ...

definitions.text: valedictory Western role for Monroe or Gable

blocks.note: first meaning: a nonconformist who does not fit in

blocks.clueFragment: valedictory Western role for Monroe or Gable
blocks.note: second meaning: both stars made their last film, a 1961 Western about wild-horse hunters, playing characters known by this title

explanation.surface: A film buff notes the last cowboy part played by two Hollywood legends, and the ellipsis runs on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The Misfits (1961) was the final completed film for both Marilyn Monroe and Clark Gable, each playing one of the title's outsiders.
explanation.definitionFit: A maverick is an individualist who stands apart from the group, just like a person who does not belong.

clue.text: ... disaster - so ran a sequel: "Here Come the Rangers!"

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer: Sloane Rangers were the posh young set named after this place

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things in a wreck, so the following words are scrambled

blocks.note: twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing from 1-down, a film flopped, yet a sequel about some rangers was rushed out anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: Sloane Rangers, the 1980s Chelsea upper-class set, took their name from SLOANE SQUARE in London, so it is where the Rangers come from.
explanation.definitionFit: The square in Chelsea gave its name to the Sloane Ranger, so the Rangers are said to come from there.

clue.text: Soft spot for bosun or midshipman?

definitions.text: Soft spot for bosun or midshipman?

blocks.clueFragment: Soft spot for bosun or midshipman
blocks.note: surface reading: a fondness someone has for sailors
setter's reading: a comfortable place to sit, like the seat a sailor might use

explanation.surface: Someone admits a weakness for naval men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft spot' means affection on the surface but literally a cushioned seat; a bosun's chair is a sailor's seat, hinting at the kind of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: An upholstered armchair is a soft place to sit and relax in comfort.

clue.text: Evidence of confinement with hard labour

definitions.text: Evidence of confinement with hard labour

blocks.clueFragment: Evidence of confinement with hard labour
blocks.note: surface reading: proof that someone served a prison sentence doing hard labour
setter's reading: confinement is the old word for childbirth and labour is giving birth, whose traces stay on the skin

explanation.surface: A record showing that someone was jailed and set to break rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: Confinement and labour both belong to childbirth; a stretch is also prison slang for a sentence, adding to the jail picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Pregnancy stretches the skin of the belly and leaves lasting streaks, visible proof of having carried a child.

clue.text: See 2
Tremble at fault's failing

blocks.note: first meaning: shake with fear
second meaning: what happens when a geological fault slips, the ground shakes

explanation.surface: Someone shakes with fear on being told of a mistake they made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fault' looks like a personal mistake, but here it is a crack in the earth's crust.
explanation.definitionFit: To shake or shudder, and also an earth tremor caused when rock along a fault suddenly gives way.

clue.text: What inspired pin-up to enter love feast?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upward
one piece goes inside another, entering it

blocks.note: the agape is the early Christian love feast
taken as written

explanation.surface: A query about what a pin-up model might have to do with a romantic banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pin-up' looks like a glamour photo but splits into pin and up. AGANIPPE was the spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinking from this fountain on Helicon was said to give poetic inspiration, as it belonged to the Muses.

clue.text: Roger eagerly brewing tea for this prime minister

indicators.note: brewing stirs ingredients together, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: in radio talk roger means received, abbreviated R
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Roger is keen to make a pot of tea in honour of a prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works both ways: EARL GREY is a bergamot tea named after the 2nd Earl Grey, prime minister in the 1830s.
explanation.definitionFit: The bergamot-scented blend carries the name of the nineteenth-century statesman who led the government and passed the Reform Act.

clue.text: Original Koppites, given to wit, round on exploiters

blocks.note: abbreviation of scilicet, Latin for namely
a round shape is the letter O
people who exploit others use them

explanation.surface: The first fans on the Kop were witty, turning on those who took advantage of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kop is the famous stand at Liverpool FC's Anfield ground; people from Liverpool are called SCOUSERS. 'On' just means the pieces follow one another.
explanation.definitionFit: The first terrace supporters at Anfield were natives of Liverpool, whose locals carry that nickname.

clue.text: Outlet where Samson was eyeless, headless and confined by lawyers

indicators.note: with no head, the first letter of the place is cut off
being confined means held inside something else

blocks.note: barristers collectively are the Bar
Milton's Samson was 'Eyeless in Gaza', the city where he was blinded

explanation.surface: Telling the Bible story of blinded Samson, beheaded and held by the legal profession.
explanation.walkthrough: Samson Agonistes has Samson 'Eyeless in Gaza'; 'eyeless' points to the city, and 'headless' drops its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A market or charity sale is a place where goods are sold, a retail outlet.

clue.text: How soon will women combine with unity? An enigma

definitions.note: the answer replies to the question rather than being a synonym of it

indicators.note: an enigma is a puzzle, so the words before it are jumbled into a riddle

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks when women will unite, a question that remains a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Combine with' looks like the anagram signal but only joins the fodder; the signal is 'enigma' at the end, with 'An' as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the natural reply to a question about timing, meaning very shortly or imminently.

clue.text: No opening for cyber-physiological style?

indicators.note: without an opening, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a body enhanced by electronic or mechanical parts is described this way

explanation.surface: A question whether there is any job for a cyborg-like fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like a vacancy, but it means the first letter. IONIC is one of the classical orders of Greek architecture.
explanation.definitionFit: The classical order with scroll-shaped capitals is an architectural manner of building columns.

clue.text: Contract bidding

blocks.note: surface reading: the auction stage of the card game contract bridge
setter's reading: making formal offers to win a business contract

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like a bridge term, but a firm competing for work submits offers in a formal process.
explanation.definitionFit: Companies submit priced offers to win a job, and that formal process of making offers is what the word names.

clue.text: Cave in Bethlehem, one up a diversion, taking one hour

indicators.note: a diversion sends things off their usual route, so the letters are rearranged
taking something away removes it from the collected letters

blocks.note: taken as written
Roman numeral one
taken as written
taken as written
a single H, the abbreviation for hour, which is removed

explanation.surface: Directions to a grotto in Bethlehem, up a detour, taking an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one of the two Hs in Bethlehem goes, as 'one hour' says. 'Cave in' looks like a grotto in the town but means to give way.
explanation.definitionFit: To back down and admit being wrong, submitting humbly after defeat, is to give way or yield.

clue.text: The first murderer slept here?

blocks.note: surface reading: like a 'Washington slept here' plaque for Cain, the first killer in Genesis
setter's reading: Genesis says Cain went to live east of Eden in a land whose name means a nod, as in dozing

explanation.walkthrough: Cain, the first murderer, settled in the land of Nod in Genesis 4; nodding off is falling asleep, so the biblical place doubles as the realm of sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis Cain dwelt there after killing Abel, and the phrase is also an idiom for being asleep.

clue.text: Progressively elevating sloth in episcopal joints?

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other
in a down clue, raising the letters reads them from the bottom upward

blocks.note: a mitre is a bishop's hat and also an angled joint in woodwork
the ai is the three-toed sloth, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A satirical picture of laziness climbing gradually through the church hierarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Episcopal joints' plays on the mitre, both a bishop's hat and a carpentry joint. SERIATIM is Latin for one after another.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin adverb means point by point in a series, taking things one after another in order.

clue.text: Society meeting the objective in Merseyside

definitions.note: a place found in the county rather than a synonym for it

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for society
taken as written
the objective is the lens nearest the object in a microscope or telescope

explanation.surface: A club meets its target somewhere in the Liverpool area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Objective' looks like a goal, but it is the optical term for a lens. Merseyside is the county around Liverpool, and ST HELENS is a town there.
explanation.definitionFit: The glassmaking town lies within the metropolitan county around Liverpool, so it is a place there.

clue.text: Slaying one gannet; one tern revived

indicators.note: brought back to life in a new form, so the letters reappear rearranged

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
taken as written
Roman numeral one again
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seabird kills a gannet, while a tern is brought round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slaying' looks like killing, which fits the birds, but in slang to slay someone is to make them laugh helplessly.
explanation.definitionFit: To slay an audience is informally to amuse it enormously, so slaying means hugely amusing.

clue.text: Hot, wearing bikini in Scotland

definitions.note: a region found in the country rather than a synonym for it

indicators.note: something worn is surrounded by the wearer, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: Bikini is a Pacific atoll, the site of nuclear tests
H is the abbreviation for hot on taps

explanation.surface: Someone sweltering in swimwear somewhere north of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bikini' is not the swimsuit but the atoll it was named after. ATHOLL is a district of Perthshire in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The highland district in Perthshire, home of the Duke of Atholl, is a region located there.

clue.text: Eleven as one

blocks.note: first meaning: a football side such as Manchester's or Leeds', commonly named this way
second meaning: joined together, in agreement

explanation.walkthrough: An eleven is a football team, and many clubs carry this word in their name, so it stands for the team.
explanation.definitionFit: Many football clubs carry the word in their name, and it also means joined together in harmony.

clue.text: Kicked by departing Inuit, was it?

definitions.text: Kicked by departing Inuit, was it?

blocks.note: surface reading: something an Inuk struck with a foot while leaving
setter's reading: to kick the bucket is to die, so a dying Arctic dweller would kick a frozen one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Departing' means dying, and 'kick the bucket' is the idiom; for someone living among snow and ice the bucket kicked would be a frozen one.
explanation.definitionFit: The container for chilling drinks is reimagined as the receptacle an Arctic dweller kicks when dying.

clue.text: A French precipitation, they say, is hardly the thing

indicators.note: what people say is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: the French for a
dew is moisture that forms on cold surfaces

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain French rainfall is not quite proper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Precipitation' suggests rain, but it is the dew that settles overnight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something excessive or improper is not the right thing, not called for, so hardly the done thing.

clue.text: Joe of 18 26 (abbr.) 2

blocks.note: surface reading: a string of cross-references to other entries in the grid
setter's reading: put the answers at 18, 26 shortened, and 2 together to get a play title, whose author is the Joe wanted

explanation.walkthrough: 18 is ENTERTAINING, 26 abbreviated is MR, and 2 is SLOANE: Entertaining Mr Sloane (1964) is the play by Joe ORTON.
explanation.definitionFit: The English playwright Joe Orton wrote the black comedy Entertaining Mr Sloane, his first big stage success.

clue.text: Last attempt to go out with it

indicators.note: going around the outside means one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a try is an attempt
the last part is the end

explanation.surface: A final effort to go out on a date with someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With it' looks like the end of a phrase about going out, but it is the definition, slang for fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being with it is informal for being up to date and fashionable, which is the same as stylish.

clue.text: Like a fiddler's elbow in a donut blender

indicators.note: a blender mixes whatever is put into it

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A violinist's jerking arm is compared to something whizzing round in a kitchen mixer.
explanation.walkthrough: A fiddler's elbow moves to and fro with the bow, the classic image of constant back-and-forth movement.
explanation.definitionFit: A violinist's bowing arm keeps moving forward and back, so it goes repeatedly to and fro.

clue.text: What-d'you-call-'im's spray gun?

blocks.note: first meaning: the form of address used for a man whose name you do not know
second meaning: a device that sprays a fine mist

explanation.surface: Asking about the spray gun belonging to some man whose name escapes you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What-d'you-call-'im' is a forgotten name; addressing an unknown man you might say 'Hey, mister!'
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title for an unnamed man and also a gadget that produces a fine mist of water.

clue.text: Bound to give the baby a squeeze

definitions.text: Bound to give the baby a squeeze

blocks.clueFragment: Bound to give the baby a squeeze
blocks.note: surface reading: certain to hug the infant
setter's reading: bound means tied up, here wrapped tightly in cloth around a newborn

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' looks like 'certain to', but bound is a past participle meaning wrapped up, as newborns traditionally were.
explanation.definitionFit: A newborn wrapped tightly in strips of cloth is snugly tied up, held firmly by the bands.
